title: Minimum Total Operations
statement:
You may apply as many operations as you like to the integer array `nums`. One operation chooses a prefix of `nums` (its first `i` elements, for any `i` from `1` to `nums.length`) and any integer `k` (it may be negative), then adds `k` to every element of that prefix.

Return the fewest operations that leave every element of `nums` with the same value.
notes:
## Intuition

Look at the gaps between neighbours. Adding `k` to the prefix that ends at index `i` moves `nums[0..i]` together, so every gap inside that prefix stays the same, and so does every gap further right. Only the gap between `nums[i]` and `nums[i + 1]` changes. All elements are equal exactly when every gap is zero, so each unequal neighbouring pair needs an operation of its own, and one operation per pair is enough.

A brute force would search over sequences of operations, which grows exponentially. The greedy sweep needs no search: aim for the value of the last element, which never has to move, and walk leftwards fixing each element that differs from its right neighbour.

## Approach

1. Let `n` be the length of `nums` and start `operations` at `0`.
2. Walk `i` from `n - 2` down to `0`, looking at the pair `nums[i]`, `nums[i + 1]`.
3. If the two differ, one operation on the prefix ending at `i` lines `nums[i]` up with everything to its right, so count it. Every earlier operation shifted both elements by the same amount, so the original values decide and the array never has to change.
4. Return `operations`.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [1, 4, 2]` and `n = 3`. At `i = 1`, `4 !== 2`: adding `-2` to the prefix `[1, 4]` gives `[-1, 2, 2]`, so `operations = 1`. At `i = 0`, `1 !== 4` (and the current `-1` and `2` are still 3 apart): adding `3` to `[-1]` gives `[2, 2, 2]`, so `operations = 2`. The answer is `2`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): one comparison per neighbouring pair.
- Space: O(1): only a counter.

## Pitfalls

- Counting distinct values fails: `[1, 2, 1]` holds only two values, but both of its gaps are nonzero, so it needs 2 operations.
- Counting the elements that differ from the last one fails on the same array: only one element differs, yet two operations are needed.
- Adding to the whole array (the prefix of length `n`) never helps, because it keeps every gap; a single element or an all-equal array needs `0`.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `n` | length of `nums` |
| `operations` | operations counted so far |
| `i` | index of the left element of the pair being compared |

narration.2: n is the number of elements; the last one, nums[n - 1], never has to move.
narration.3: operations counts the operations the sweep uses.
narration.4: Walk the neighbouring pairs from the right end towards the start.
narration.5: Do nums[i] and its right neighbour differ? Earlier operations shifted both by the same amount, so the original values decide.
narration.6: Yes: one operation on the prefix ending at i lines it up with everything to its right.
narration.9: Every unequal neighbouring pair cost exactly one operation, and none could be skipped.
